title: Restrictions on non-Clifford fault tolerance and ruling out beyond-SQL quantum metrology
authors: Constantin Cedillo Vayson de Pradenne, Ishaan Kannan, Harald Putterman, Jordan Cotler
abstract: Quantum metrology promises a quadratic speedup over the standard quantum limit (SQL), but signal-aligned noise is expected to preclude this advantage in realistic settings. A potential route around known no-go results is to encode the sensors in a quantum code where the physical signal acts transversally as a logical gate. Understanding restrictions on transversal non-Clifford gates is therefore central to both quantum metrology and fault-tolerant quantum computation. Here, we prove such restrictions and apply them to transversal sensing. For any stabilizer code of distance $d\ge 3$ supporting a transversal logical action in level $D$ of the Clifford hierarchy, every stabilizer generating set must contain a check of weight at least $2^D$. Moreover, any $r$-level concatenated realization satisfies $r\leq \lfloor \log_2 n/D\rfloor$, forcing $r=1$ and ruling out concatenation when applied to beyond-SQL metrology. We then show that transversal single-qubit rotations by a small angle $θ$ can only induce a nontrivial logical action on an $n$-qubit code if its checks include irreducible stabilizers of weight $Ω(1/(n|θ|^2))$. Here, many single-qubit errors commute with every stabilizer or logical Pauli below this weight and are only detected by a high-weight check, so their syndromes cannot be fault-tolerantly reconstructed from low-weight normalizer measurements. Since beyond-SQL transversal sensing requires $|θ| = o(n^{-1/2})$, the weight of checks required for syndrome extraction diverges with $n$. Finally, we prove a broader metrological no-go theorem that avoids the assumptions of the quantum Cramér-Rao bound: constant-strength signal-aligned noise rules out any asymptotic advantage over the SQL in AC or DC sensing, even with biased estimators, nonstabilizer or approximate encodings, quantum memory, intermediate measurements, or adaptive control.
summary: This paper rigorously proves severe limitations on achieving super-classical sensitivity in quantum metrology. It shows that for signal noise correlated with the measurement signal, any attempt to surpass the Standard Quantum Limit requires an exponentially growing resource (check weight) incompatible with fault-tolerant encoding. The work establishes a general no-go theorem ruling out such advantages under realistic noise conditions.
main_problem: The paper investigates fundamental restrictions on implementing non-Clifford gates fault-tolerantly and proves a general no-go theorem ruling out asymptotic quantum metrological advantages beyond the Standard Quantum Limit (SQL) when signal noise is aligned.
main_result: It establishes that achieving beyond-SQL sensing requires stabilizer checks whose weight diverges with system size, and more broadly, constant-strength signal-aligned noise prevents any asymptotic speedup over the SQL in AC or DC sensing.
method: The authors use rigorous mathematical proofs based on properties of stabilizer codes, analyzing code susceptibility ($\Xi_G$), Bures distance bounds derived from quantum channels, and comparing required error correction weights against achievable scaling laws.
model_or_system: The model involves encoding quantum sensors in Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs) to measure a physical signal Hamiltonian ($H$). The analysis considers protocols under realistic noise models, including dephasing ($\gamma$) and erasure channels ($p_e$), particularly when the signal coupling is aligned with the noise generators.

important_parameters: Code distance ($d\ge 3$), logical gate level ($D$), noise strengths ($\gamma, p_e$), and the scaling exponent $\alpha$ governing the desired metrological advantage.
main_assumptions: The strongest results rely on the assumption that signal-aligned noise (noise sharing Pauli generators with the signal) is present. The analysis also considers various advanced techniques like biased estimators or nonstabilizer encodings in the final theorem.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Heisenberg-limited sensing and fault-tolerance obstructions, showing that high speedup requires checks of polynomially growing weight, which conflicts with local noise assumptions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first deriving quantitative restrictions on transversal non-Clifford gates (Theorem 1), then analyzing the limitations imposed on concatenated codes (Theorem 2), applying these to single-qubit rotations (Theorem 3), and culminating in a general no-go theorem for metrology under signal-aligned noise (Theorem 5).
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental theoretical constraints on quantum sensing, showing that realistic noise models severely limit the achievable precision scaling, even when using sophisticated error correction techniques.
